findings.heading: Preparation > Packages
findings.proposition: The prose says the chunk demonstrates pacman's `p_load_gh()` to install and load a GitHub package, but the French chunk (lines 40-65) uses `if(!require(sitrep)){ remotes::install_github("r4epi/sitrep"); library(sitrep) }` and never calls `p_load_gh()`.
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader looks in the chunk for the `p_load_gh()` call the text promises, does not find it, and cannot learn the pacman GitHub idiom the section exists to teach; they may also assume **remotes** is unnecessary when the shown code requires it.

findings.heading: Observation time
findings.proposition: The English defines the recall period as the time that participants are asked to report on when answering questions; the French defines it as 'le moment où l'enquête est menée' (the moment when the survey is conducted).
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader takes the recall period to be the fieldwork date rather than the retrospective window, so they set `recall_start`/`recall_end` to the survey dates and compute person-time and mortality rates over the wrong period.

findings.heading: Observation time
findings.proposition: The English states that the end date is the earliest appropriate departure event within the recall period; the French 'Date de fin' block omits this defining line entirely.
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader loses the rule that defines the end date, so they cannot see why `find_end_date()` picks the earliest departure event and may take a later departure, inflating observation time.

findings.heading: Observation time
findings.proposition: The English qualifies the pre-recall-end date with 'if applicable (e.g. departures, deaths)'; the French sentence stops at 'une date antérieure à la fin du rappel' and gives no examples or condition.
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader does not learn which events (departures, deaths) can end observation before the recall end, so they may fail to treat deaths and departures as end-date causes when adapting the code.

findings.heading: Survey design objects > Srvyr package
findings.proposition: The English says `as_survey_design()` allows pipes (`%>%`) so the tilde (`~`) is not needed; the French writes the tilde as `%>%`: 'nous n'avons donc pas besoin d'utiliser le tilde (`%>%`)'.
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader is told the pipe both is allowed and is not needed in the same sentence, and never learns that `~` is the symbol dropped when moving from `svydesign()` to `as_survey_design()`.

findings.heading: Descriptive analysis > Demographic pyramids
findings.proposition: The English recommends creating descriptive tables of age and sex by survey strata; the French reads 'des tableaux descriptifs et le sexe par strates d'enquête' and drops age from the recommendation.
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader tabulates only sex by stratum and omits the age distribution, which is the variable the age pyramid and the sampling-bias check both depend on.

findings.heading: Weighted proportions > Survey package
findings.proposition: The English states that an appropriate design effect is extracted with `svymean()` rather than `svyciprop()`; the French omits this sentence.
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader does not learn which function yields the design effect, so when the chunk calls `svymean()` alongside `svyciprop()` they cannot tell why, and may try to read a design effect off `svyciprop()`.
